claims.text: Equiatomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has very limited room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has previously been inferred computationally rather than established experimentally.
Adding approximately 5 at% Ti and applying thermomechanical processing will induce an inverted dual-phase microstructure in NbMoTaW.
The proposed microstructure will consist of a continuous ductile BCC matrix containing finely distributed Ti-rich precipitates.

An inverted microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and nanoscale precipitates can improve room-temperature ductility while retaining substantial yield strength in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The fine precipitates will impede crack propagation during mechanical loading.
The interfaces associated with the proposed precipitates will act as irradiation-defect sinks.
Ti addition will increase local lattice distortion and alter defect energetics in NbMoTaW.
The Ti-induced changes in lattice distortion and defect energetics will promote nucleation of ductile regions or fine precipitates.
The proposed microstructural features will enhance dislocation mobility.
Additional interfaces will enhance vacancy-interstitial recombination under irradiation.
Enhanced defect recombination will reduce irradiation-induced defect clustering, helium blistering, and amorphization.
Maintaining a dominant BCC network will preserve high-temperature strength.
The Ti-modified alloy will increase room-temperature fracture strain by at least 20–50% relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will show a lower post-irradiation density of dislocation loops or irradiation-induced precipitates than untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will retain high yield and fracture strengths at temperatures up to 1600 °C.
The beneficial balance will persist under helium implantation across multiple energies and typical dpa regimes without deleterious phase transformations or excessive precipitation.
